<reason>B better defends the proposition’s actual sequencing rule: meaningful improvements in physical and shared activities, not completed facilities. A establishes genuine costs from delaying accessible digital options, but repeatedly assumes rather than demonstrates their implementation advantage. Most importantly, A’s claim that postponing digital expansion cannot benefit physical provision conflicts with its acknowledgment of scarce budgets and staff. B directly exposes this contradiction and explains why matching programs to needs does not itself resolve funding priority. B candidly accepts delay costs and provides the stronger comparative justification for bearing them.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s closing challenges A’s assertion that the programs do not compete for funding: a ready digital program still has an opportunity cost. A’s final reply acknowledges the shared budget yet insists physical provision gains nothing from digital postponement, leaving B’s central rebuttal unanswered.</best_rebuttal>
